newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Eleven months on, Israel's Netanyahu in trouble.
newsitem.headline: Eleven months on, Israel's Netanyahu in trouble.

text.p: Eleven months after roaring from behind to capture the top job in Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a corruption scandal that could catapult him from the prime minister's office to jail.

The right-wing leader has snarled peacemaking with the Arabs and presided over a sagging economy but it is his ill-fated appointment of an attorney-general in January which now threatens to topple his government.
Police recommended in a 995-page report completed this week that Netanyhau, 47, be charged with fraud and breach of trust in an influence-peddling scandal involving top officials.
Legal experts say an indictment would force Netanyahu's resignation and prompt new elections. The charge carries a maximum penalty of three years in prison.
His aides have blamed a "hostile press" and hinted at a partisan police investigation while insisting that state prosecutors, who must decide whether to charge the prime minister, will exonerate him.

Netanyahu, a former commando, unseated Labour party leader and Nobel prize laureate Shimon Peres in elections last May by fewer than 30,000 votes to become Israel's youngest and arguably most powerful prime minister.
Riding to office on a new direct election law which expanded the prime minister's powers, Netanyahu has touted the fact that his mandate comes from the people and not party bosses.

His campaign last year pledged to make Israelis secure after a wave of suicide bombings by Moslem militants, while honouring peace agreements with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) which Netanyahu never supported.
Both promises have proved hard to keep.

In September, gunbattles erupted between Israeli troops and Palestinian forces after Israel opened a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem. Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed.

Things took a hopeful turn when Netanyahu pulled Israeli troops out of most of the West Bank town of Hebron in January after months of acrimonious negotiations with the PLO, fulfilling a commitment made by the prior government.
But the recent building of a new Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem again angered Arabs and strained ties with the United States, Israel's closest ally.
Peace negotiations with the Palestinians ground to a halt when Netanyahu sent bulldozers to carve out a new Jewish settlement on a Jerusalem hilltop on March 18.
Three days later, a Palestinian bomber killed three Israeli women at a Tel Aviv cafe in what security officials warned could be the beginning of another bombing spree.
The settlement building also sparked Palestinian unrest in the West Bank reminiscent of a six-year uprising that ended with Israel's first interim peace deal with the PLO in 1993.
At home, Netanyahu has hyped plans to revive Israel's near recession economy and sell off government-owned companies but the budget deficit is off its target and inflation is climbing.

Critics viewed the appointment of Likud party activist Roni Bar-On to the post of attorney-general as part of Netanyahu's agenda to replace the "establishment elites" in the army and in public service -- people he associates with the once hegemonic Labour party -- with his own cronies.
But a television report alleging the appointment was part of a plan to win a plea-bargain for key coalition legislator Aryeh Deri, already on trial for corruption, prompted a police probe.
Their findings point to Netanyahu, his director-general, Avigdor Lieberman, Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi and Deri. Prosecutors have promised a decision on police recommendations within days.
Educated in the United States in business and architecture and a master of its political style, Netanyahu is admired by his supporters for his fluency before the cameras.
Born in Tel Aviv to an eminent historian, he was in an elite army unit from 1967 to 1972. He was shot and wounded leading commandos disguised as workers onto a commandeered Sabena airliner in 1972.
In the mid-1970s, he met Moshe Arens, a Likud parliamentarian who became his mentor.
He was the Likud government's champion of the airwaves in the 1991 Gulf War and later that year at the historic launching of peace talks with the Palestinians, Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan in Madrid.
After Likud's defeat in the 1992 Israeli election, Netanyahu was chosen new party leader and orchestrated its return to power.
